prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s my belief that every man Should do his share of work, And in our economic plan No citizen should shirk. That in return each one should get His meed of fold and food, And feel that all his toil and sweat Is for the common good. It’s my belief that every chap Should have an equal start, And there should be no handicap To hinder his depart; That there be fairness in the fight, And justice in the race, And every lad should have the right To win his proper place. It’s my belief that people should Be neither rich nor poor; That none should suffer servitude, And all should be secure. That wealth is loot, and rank is rot, And foul is class and clan; That to succeed a man may not Exploit his brother man. It’s my belief that heritage And usury are wrong; That each should win a worthy wage And sing an honest song .... Not one like this — for though I rue The wrong of life, I flout it. Alas! I’m not prepared to do A goddam thing about it.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Should, And, That

outputs.L1:
Here are two polished options depending on your intended context. 

### Option 1: Professional Prose Statement
*Best for formal essays, speeches, or professional articles.*

> I firmly hold that every individual must contribute their fair share of labor to our shared economic framework, without exception. In return, every worker is entitled to equitable compensation and basic sustenance, accompanied by the assurance that their hard work advances the common good. 
> 
> I believe in genuine equality of opportunity from the very start, unburdened by systemic handicaps or arbitrary barriers. True justice demands a fair field where every person has the right to achieve their earned potential. 
> 
> Furthermore, society should tolerate neither extreme wealth nor deep poverty; all citizens deserve security, and none should endure servitude. I view hoarded wealth and rigid class hierarchies as fundamentally corrupt, for true success can never be built on the exploitation of others. Generational privilege and predatory financial practices are inherently unjust; every individual deserves a dignified, worthy wage for honest effort. 
> 
> Yet, while I deeply lament these societal flaws, I must confess to a fundamental irony: despite my indignation, I am entirely unprepared to take any meaningful action to remedy them.

***

### Option 2: Elevated Rhetorical Verse
*Retains the rhythmic feel and poetic structure of the original while refining the tone and vocabulary.*

> It is my conviction that every person should do their part,  
> And within our economic framework, no citizen should shirk.  
> In return, each should receive a fair share of sustenance and reward,  
> Knowing that their toil serves the greater good.  
> 
> I believe that everyone deserves an equal starting line,  
> Free from handicaps that impede their progress.  
> Let fairness govern the struggle and justice guide the race,  
> So that every individual may earn their rightful place.  
> 
> I hold that society should know neither luxury nor destitute poverty;  
> That none should endure servitude, and all should be secure.  
> For excessive wealth is plunder, class distinction is corrupt,  
> And no person should succeed by exploiting their fellow man.  
> 
> Inherited privilege and predatory usury are wrong;  
> Every worker deserves a worthy wage and a life of honest endeavor.  
> Yet, though I mourn the inequities of this life, I merely flout them—  
> For alas, I am entirely unprepared to do a single thing about it.
outputs.L2:
Here is a complete paraphrase of the passage, maintaining all the original ideas while using fresh phrasing and structure:

I hold the conviction that every single person ought to contribute their fair share of labor, leaving no room for slackers within a society's economic framework. In exchange for their hard work, every individual deserves a proper share of basic necessities and compensation, alongside the satisfaction of knowing their efforts serve the collective well-being. 

Furthermore, I maintain that everyone should be granted an identical starting point in life, unburdened by unfair obstacles that might impede their progress. Life's struggles and competitions must be governed by justice and impartiality, ensuring that every young person possesses the genuine right to earn the standing they deserve.

I also believe that severe wealth disparities should not exist—no one should be excessively wealthy or languish in poverty. Society should offer complete security to all while entirely eliminating any form of bondage. In my view, hoarded fortunes are essentially stolen goods, social titles are worthless, and class divisions are toxic. Ultimately, no one should ever achieve personal success by taking advantage of their fellow human beings.

It is my firm stance that generational wealth transfers and charging interest on loans are fundamentally unethical. Instead, every person ought to earn a respectable living through truthful and honorable means. 

However, I must admit the truth about verses like this: while I deeply regret the unfairness of the world, I ultimately dismiss it. Regrettably, I am completely unwilling to lift a finger to change any of it.
outputs.L3:
At the heart of a flourishing civilization lies a fundamental pact: every citizen should contribute to the collective strength of society through their own labor, receiving fair compensation that honors their effort and serves the common good. Work ought to be a source of personal dignity and societal progress, ensuring that the wealth generated by human hands and minds is shared equitably rather than hoarded selfishly.

To realize such a society, every individual deserves a genuinely equal start in life. True justice demands an uncompromised baseline of opportunity, where a person’s potential is never limited by the circumstances of their birth, class barriers, or unfair systemic handicaps. Success should be the product of individual merit and honest dedication, not the fortunate accident of coming from a privileged lineage.

Consequently, a moral economic system must actively work to eliminate the destructive extremes of human condition: the obscene concentration of wealth on one end, and degrading poverty on the other. Preventing the exploitation of workers is essential to ensuring that every household enjoys basic economic security. Furthermore, practices such as unearned inherited privilege and predatory financial usury are fundamentally unethical; they distort the economy and undermine the foundational principle that prosperity should be earned through honest, productive work.

In theory, these principles form the bedrock of an ideal blueprint for human social justice. In practice, however, I must candidly admit that I am entirely unwilling to do anything to bring this vision to fruition. While I hold these convictions with absolute intellectual enthusiasm, I lack any desire to organize, protest, push for policy reform, or sacrifice my personal comfort for the cause. I am, ultimately, content to remain a passive spectator—holding profound utopian ideals while remaining completely, unapologetically steadfast in my own inertia.
outputs.L4:
**Manifesto from the Chaise Longue**

Let the towers of capital crumble to dust,
Where the few hoard the gold while the many eat rust!
Why should one man be born to a velvet-lined throne,
While a thousand must bleed just to harvest a stone?
No—the earth is a garden belonging to all,
And the higher the fortress, the steeper the fall.

We must tear down the hedges and burn down the gates,
Erase every border that isolates states,
And dismantle the ladder of lineage and lord,
Till the sweat of the brow is the only reward.
Let the burden of labor be equally shared:
Let the CEO toil where the cobblestones cleared,
Let the doctor, the miner, the clerk, and the chef
Find their compensation no longer bereft
Of the dignity owed to the work of their hands—
A single, fair wage across all of our lands.

No privilege of birth! No inherited claim!
No system that prospers on poverty’s shame!
Rise up, O ye masses, take hold of the dawn!
The age of the tyrant is bloody and gone!
Together we’ll march till the dawn breaks anew,
And build a bright future for me and for you!

…Or at least, so I’d say, if the weather were clear,
But it’s drizzling outside, and I’m comfortable here.
Besides, I’ve a slight, nagging ache in my knee,
And I’m halfway through drinking a hot cup of tea. 

Yes, someone should really go march in the street,
To confront the police and endure all the heat!
I’d be right by your side, but I’m drafting a post
On the subtle nuance of the oligarch’s boast;
It’s a vital critique of late-stage capitalism,
Which I’ll publish online between breakfast and schism. 

So tear down the system! Demand what is right!
I am with you in spirit throughout the whole fight.
Go alter the world! Make the centuries yield!
(Just don't ask me to personally step in the field.)
I’ll cheer from the sofa, entirely devout,
And repost the photos when you sort it all out.
outputs.L5:
Every day, we find ourselves navigating a quiet tension between who we are and who the world expects us to be. We are constantly surrounded by unspoken rules detailing what we **should** achieve, how we ought to act, and which paths are deemed worthy of success. Yet, living entirely by the expectations of others often leads to a life that feels borrowed rather than earned.

Real growth requires a willingness to look beyond these rigid boundaries **and** embrace the uncertainty that comes with forging our own way. It demands that we balance ambition with self-compassion, understanding that progress is rarely a straight line. 

Ultimately, it is **that** willingness to listen to our own inner voice—rather than the noise around us—that defines the quality of our journey. When we align our choices with our deepest values, we stop merely reacting to life and begin truly living it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical, rhyming poem about an armchair revolutionary who preaches socialist values and economic equality, but ultimately admits at the very end that they are too lazy to do anything about it.
counterfactuals.output:
Awake, ye wretched of the earth! The time has come to rise!
We must tear down the corporate gods and cut them down to size!
The proletariat shall reign! The top one percent must pay!
We’ll seize the means of production without a moment’s delay!

I preach the gospel of the red, I champion the mass,
I spit upon the landlords and the parasitic class.
I quote from Marx, I tweet from Engels, fiercely I debate
On how late-stage capitalism doomed the modern state.

I post long rants on social apps from cozy velvet chairs,
Decrying all the CEOs and greedy billionaires.
I sip a customized espresso, scowl at every yacht,
And draft my fiery manifestos from a comfy spot.

The barricades are calling out! The workers must unite!
It’s time to burn the system down and step into the light!
Go march into the city square! Go tear the fences down!
Reclaim the wealth for everyone in every single town!

Yes, strike the blow! Reclaim the streets! Go join the grand crusade!
(Just leave me out of it, my friends, I’m staying in the shade).
For though my heart bleeds for the poor, my sofa is too deep,
And overthrowing government would ruin my morning sleep.

I’d gladly march beside you all to make the tyrants bleed,
But putting on my shoes today is more effort than I need.
The class war sounds inspiring, but it’s drizzling out today—
So go and free the masses, guys! I’ll cheer you from my duvet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you share the text of the poem "My Belief" by Robert W. Service?
counterfactuals.output:
Here is the poem **"My Belief"** by Robert W. Service:

***

### My Belief
**By Robert W. Service**

It's my belief that after all
The world is pretty good;
That though we stumble and we fall,
We'd all do better if we could.
That spite of war and greed and crime,
And human misery and tears,
We're climbing upward all the time,
And bettering with the years.

It's my belief that God is kind,
And loves us every one;
That though we're foolish, weak and blind,
He will not leave a thing undone
To help us in our hour of need,
To comfort us in our distress,
Regardless of our race or creed,
Or whether we've failure or success.

It's my belief that love is king,
And kindness is his queen;
That every good and gracious thing
Is better than the mean.
That spite of evil, sin and strife,
The dark and cruel things we see,
The final goal of human life
Is love and light and liberty.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem outlining a high-minded political philosophy regarding equal opportunity, fair labor, and abolishing class structures, concluding with a funny punchline that reveals the speaker's utter apathy.
counterfactuals.output:
Upon the altar of the common good,
We must dismantle every tower of greed,
Where lords of capital have long withstood
The desperate cries of those in bitter need.

No child should bear the shadow of their birth,
Nor privilege dictate the path they tread;
Equal opportunity must span the earth,
With dignity in work for daily bread.

The fruits of labor belong to those who toil,
Not oligarchs upon their gilded thrones!
We’ll tear the wealthy’s grip from off the soil,
And crush the class divide to dust and stones!

A grand utopia where all are free,
Where equity and justice reign supreme!
A shining dawn of true fraternity!
A noble, necessary, glorious dream!

So rise up, comrades! Break the tyrant’s trap!
Or don't. I really don't care. I'm taking a nap.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a funny poem about someone who passionately decries the injustices of the world and capitalism, but is too comfortable or hypocritical to actually be part of the solution.
counterfactuals.output:
Sebastian reposed on his mid-century chair,
With a dramatic sigh and a toss of his hair.
He opened his laptop—the sleek, latest screen—
To rail at the evils of the corporate machine.

"Down with the bosses! The billionaires must fall!
Late-stage capitalism is crushing us all!
We must seize the means! We must burn down the state!"
He typed with a fury, a passion, a hate.

He paused for a moment to sip his cold brew,
Double-shot, oat milk, artisanal too.
Delivered by DoorDash (he tipped fifty cents),
While raging on Twitter at high city rents.

"Rise up, my comrades! To arms in the street!"
He posted in caps from his duvet so sweet.
His iPhone was warm in his velvet-clad palm,
As he bought some bamboo-scented soap to stay calm.

"There’s a strike at the warehouse!" his buddy declared,
"Let’s go hold a sign, show the workers we cared!"
Sebastian just winced and looked out at the sky:
"Oh, man, I’d be there, but the humidity's high..."

"And my yoga starts soon, then my Pilates at four,
Plus I’m waiting for Amazon right at my door—
I ordered a hoodie that says *EAT THE RICH*,
It was ninety-five bucks, but it has a nice stitch!"

"Besides," he reasoned, "my duty is clear:
I’m fighting the *mind-wars*, the digital sphere!
If I go outside and get wet in the rain,
Who’s left to post memes about corporate pain?"

So he liked three infographics, gave a passionate retweet,
From the temp-controlled comfort of his window seat.
A warrior for justice, a champion of truth,
Smashing the system... from a velvet-lined booth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a ballad in the style of Robert W. Service about socio-economic fairness that turns from a serious idealist rant into a humorous confession of inactive defeatism.
counterfactuals.output:
There are monstrous sins in the gilded dens where the lords of lucre reign,
While the broken throng in the slush along are bound by an iron chain.
I sat one night by a flickering light, and my soul was scorched with hate,
At the corporate few who skim the dew while the millions curse their fate.

"Oh, the world is bent by the one percent!" I roared to the midnight air,
"They have bought the laws with their greedy claws and left the cupboards bare!
Why should one fat slick wear a golden brick while the honest worker dies?
It’s a rotten game, it’s a burning shame, and it’s time the mob should rise!"

I slammed my fist on the table edge and I swore by the frozen stars,
That we’d break the locks of the Wall Street blocks and smash through the iron bars.
We must seize the land with a righteous hand! We must make the fat cats pay!
Let the workers unite in the blinding light of a bright new social day!

"To the barricades!" was my battle-cry, "To the streets with pike and flame!
We shall march en masse through the icy pass to avenge the people's name!
We will tear them down from the tower top, we will strip their velvet coats!"
And my heart beat fast like a bugle blast with the anger in my throat.

So I stood straight up with my spirit fierce, and I reached to grab my cap,
When a draft crept in through the floorboard thin, and it gave my knee a slap.
And I looked out wide at the dark outside, where the wind was howling deep,
And a quiet thought in my brain was caught: *Man, it’s cold, and I want to sleep.*

Now, I’m with the mass, and I hate the class that hoards all the earthly dough,
And I thoroughly mean to be brave and lean... but it’s twenty-two below.
And a revolution, I’ve heard it said, takes a lot of standing 'round,
And my boots are old, and the pavement’s cold, and my sciatica’s profound.

Besides, my radiator’s humming nice, and my flannel pants are warm,
And it seems a shame to expose my frame to the rigor of the storm.
So I’ll fire off a scathing post online—a sharp, rebellious tweet!
That will surely shatter the plutocrats in their high-and-mighty seat.

Yes, the fight is just, and smash them we must—of that I have no doubt!
(Though I do hope somebody cleans it up when the rioting burns out).
So march, ye brave, to the tyrant's grave! Go strike for the common good!
I’ll be right back here with a takeout beer, revolting... from the neighborhood.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
